## Reading verification evidence

Verification asks whether the implementation solves its stated discrete problem. This chapter separates
an assertion in source, an independent algebra check and a measured execution of a pinned build.
A tolerance is an acceptance criterion; it is not an observed error.

### Derivation

#### Why a volume-weighted conservation check is necessary

Take a fixed, one-dimensional column with no mass source. Total density is $\rho$ in
$\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, velocity is $v_1$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, cell volume is $V_i$ in
$\mathrm{m^3}$ and face area is $A_{i\pm1/2}$ in $\mathrm{m^2}$.
With $\mathbf n$ the dimensionless outward unit normal, the continuity equation and its volume integral are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf v)&=0,\\
\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V_i}\rho\,dV
  &=-\int_{\partial V_i}\rho\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n\,dA.
\end{aligned}
$$

For a column, assume that the lateral boundary contributes
no mass flux. Let $F_{i\pm1/2}$ denote the numerical total-mass flux density in
$\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, oriented toward increasing $x_1$.
Replace each face integral by its area times the numerical face-average flux. With fixed volumes,
$\bar\rho_i$ is the stored density average and a dot denotes its semidiscrete time derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_i\dot{\bar\rho}_i
 &=-A_{i+1/2}F_{i+1/2}+A_{i-1/2}F_{i-1/2},\\
\dot{\bar\rho}_i
 &=-\frac{\Delta_i[AF]}{V_i}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The positive face difference divided by volume is the operator in `CoordinateImpl::divergence`
({{< code src/coord/coordinate.cpp CoordinateImpl::divergence >}}).
The statement here concerns that flux-form operator; it does not claim a particular reconstruction order.

Sum adjacent cells before evaluating a relative error. The upper-face contribution of one cell and the
lower-face contribution of its neighbour have the same area and flux and opposite signs:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_i\dot{\bar\rho}_i+V_{i+1}\dot{\bar\rho}_{i+1}
 &= A_{i-1/2}F_{i-1/2}-A_{i+1/2}F_{i+1/2}\\
 &\qquad +A_{i+1/2}F_{i+1/2}-A_{i+3/2}F_{i+3/2},\\
 &= A_{i-1/2}F_{i-1/2}-A_{i+3/2}F_{i+3/2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $\mathcal I$ denote all interior cells in the column. Repeating that cancellation over every internal face gives

$$
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}V_i\dot{\bar\rho}_i=-[AF]_{\mathrm{walls}}.
$$ {#eq-ch15-budget}

The face differences in @eq-ch15-budget come from `CoordinateImpl::divergence`
({{< code src/coord/coordinate.cpp CoordinateImpl::divergence >}}).
Thus the right-hand side is zero at closed walls. The identity is exact in real arithmetic if both cells use
the same face transfer. It does not hold by cancellation when the two blocks use different seam fluxes.
Floating-point sums can leave a residual. Summing density without volumes tests a different quantity on
an unequal-volume grid. The algebra check uses unequal volumes to expose that mistake.

#### Relative drift and a zero reference

Let $\mathcal O$ be the initial, nonzero mass oracle in kilograms. The relative drift can be written either
as a difference divided by the reference magnitude or as a ratio minus one:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|\frac{\sum_i V_i\bar\rho_i}{\mathcal O}-1\right|
 &=\left|\frac{\sum_i V_i\bar\rho_i-\mathcal O}{\mathcal O}\right|,\\
 &=\frac{\left|\sum_i V_i\bar\rho_i-\mathcal O\right|}{|\mathcal O|}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The same steps apply to a nonzero energy reference in joules or a water-mass reference in kilograms.
`WallSaturation.phase_change_preserves_energy_and_water` constructs volume-weighted totals and applies
this ratio form ({{< code tests/test_wall_saturation.cpp WallSaturation.phase_change_preserves_energy_and_water >}}).
For a zero reference the division is undefined. Use an explicitly chosen dimensional absolute tolerance;
do not infer one from a relative threshold. The catalogue keeps each test's own normalization.

#### What a two-grid order estimate means

Use a fixed physical domain and uniform cell width $h_i$ in metres. Let $\mathcal O$ now denote the exact
density oracle evaluated with the same averaging convention as $\bar\rho^{(h_i)}$.
The local symbols $\nu_{15}$ (dimensionless convergence exponent) and $C_{15}>0$
(error coefficient, density units divided by $\mathrm m^{\nu_{15}}$) are proposed additions, flagged in
`ISSUES.md`. They do not reuse $p$ (pressure), $e$ (specific internal energy) or $\mathcal E$ (energy functional).

Assume a nonzero leading error with a single power over the grids being compared:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lVert\bar\rho^{(h_i)}-\mathcal O\rVert_\infty&=C_{15}h_i^{\nu_{15}},\\
\lVert\bar\rho^{(h_i/2)}-\mathcal O\rVert_\infty&=C_{15}(h_i/2)^{\nu_{15}},\\
\frac{\lVert\bar\rho^{(h_i)}-\mathcal O\rVert_\infty}
 {\lVert\bar\rho^{(h_i/2)}-\mathcal O\rVert_\infty}
 &=\frac{C_{15}h_i^{\nu_{15}}}{C_{15}h_i^{\nu_{15}}2^{-\nu_{15}}},\\
 &=2^{\nu_{15}},\\
\log_2\!\left(
\frac{\lVert\bar\rho^{(h_i)}-\mathcal O\rVert_\infty}
 {\lVert\bar\rho^{(h_i/2)}-\mathcal O\rVert_\infty}\right)&=\nu_{15}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch15-order}

The same ratio applies to a nonzero scalar face error. `faces_next_to_the_walls_are_second_order` uses
`log2(a / b)` ({{< code tests/test_wb_ref_wall.cpp faces_next_to_the_walls_are_second_order >}}).
@eq-ch15-order is exact only under the single-power assumption. Higher-order terms, temporal error and
roundoff change the measured ratio. At least three resolutions give two adjacent ratios and allow a check
that the apparent order is stabilizing. Two grids provide one estimate, not proof of an asymptotic regime.

### Numerical method

@fig-ch15-evidence separates the evidence paths. First inspect the source assertion and the registration.
Next verify the binary or package origin. Then run the selected arm and preserve passes, failures and skips.
Record the full code commit, deck, compiler and library versions, precision, device, process count and environment.


### Limits

Exact algebra cannot establish device parity, communication correctness, nonlinear stability or physical
validation. The catalogue states selected acceptance contracts, not an exhaustive coverage matrix.
The independent report checks can also fail because a stored output contains machine-dependent roundoff digits;
inspect the residual and its bound before interpreting that as a failed physical identity.
